title: Can the Treasury think long-term on climate and nature?
label: 4 November 2026 · Treasury, climate and nature
summary: The committee questioned Jill Rutter and Professor Michael Jacobs about whether HM Treasury’s focus on fiscal control and short-term Budget processes blocks long-term investment in climate adaptation and nature recovery. Witnesses said the Treasury’s power and the Budget process can disrupt long-term plans, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) and scoring rules bias short horizons, and better cross-departmental institutions, clearer targets, and new budgeting tools are needed to align investment with long-term climate and nature goals.

speakers.label: Professor Jacobs
speakers.name: Professor Michael Jacobs
speakers.role: Emeritus Professor of Political Economy, University of Sheffield; Visiting Professor, LSE

glossary.definition: The Chancellor’s annual fiscal statement and package of tax and spending decisions, with quick enactment and limited external scrutiny.
The Treasury guidance on how government appraises public projects, including value-for-money tests.
Office for Budget Responsibility, the public body that scores fiscal policies and produces fiscal forecasts.
The UK law (2008) that sets legally binding carbon budgets and targets.
The 2021 law that sets environmental targets, which are not legally enforced in the same way as carbon budgets.

glossary.term: Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet
glossary.definition: A new central unit intended to coordinate priorities and strategy across government.
The body that advises on climate adaptation under the Climate Change Act.

chapters.title: How the Treasury’s role and the Budget shape climate policy
chapters.takeaway: The Treasury’s power and the unique Budget process give it outsized influence, and that can undermine steady, long-term climate and nature investment.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Please introduce yourselves and say whether the Treasury’s focus on fiscal control stops long-term investment for climate and nature.

turns.speaker: Jill Rutter
turns.text: I’m Jill Rutter, Senior Fellow at the Institute for Government; I used to work at the Treasury and DEFRA. The Treasury isn’t opposed to long-term spending in principle, but its control of fiscal totals and short-term habits can create barriers.

turns.speaker: Jill Rutter
turns.text: The Treasury does many things beyond spending—tax, growth policy and financial services—and those other roles affect how it treats environmental spending.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We heard policy keeps changing — EV policy, the green homes grant switched off quickly — which deters investors. Do you agree?

turns.speaker: Jill Rutter
turns.text: Yes. Rapid switches harm market confidence. The green homes grant showed you need time to build accredited suppliers; turning schemes off wastes firms’ investment in skills and capacity.

turns.speaker: Professor Jacobs
turns.text: I’m Michael Jacobs. The Treasury includes officials, the Chancellor and processes. A determined Chancellor can steer things, but the Budget process is unique and problematic.

turns.speaker: Professor Jacobs
turns.text: In a Budget the Chancellor can announce tax and subsidy changes with little scrutiny, which can disrupt markets and long-term planning.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Does the Treasury’s ‘challenge’ role help or hinder when policies require big upfront spending and long-term benefits?

turns.speaker: Professor Jacobs
turns.text: Two problems: the Treasury is mainly the assessor, not the policy proposer; and short spending cycles and rules push Departments to favour things that pay off quickly rather than long-term investments.

turns.speaker: Jill Rutter
turns.text: There have been improvements: multi-year spending rounds and a longer capital period help, and the Government reduced the discount rate to favour long-term projects. But Budget process oddities remain.

chapters.title: How fiscal scoring and the OBR bias short horizons
chapters.takeaway: The way the OBR and Treasury score policies focuses benefits into short windows, discouraging investments that pay off after five years.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: The NEF says five-year spending rules work against preventative investment. How should Ministers tackle that?

turns.speaker: Professor Jacobs
turns.text: Technically, the OBR model ignores effects beyond five years and assumes small multipliers and crowding out, so long-payoff investments look unattractive in fiscal scoring.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: So what should we recommend to Government about the OBR and scoring?

turns.speaker: Professor Jacobs
turns.text: Review the OBR’s model and its assumptions. We wrote to an expert suggesting that. This Committee suggesting a review would carry weight.

turns.speaker: Jill Rutter
turns.text: Publication of longer-term fiscal assessments would help. Government could use a 10-year projection in spending reviews so prevention benefits show up earlier.

turns.speaker: Professor Jacobs
turns.text: Also, OBR’s fiscal risks reports look long-term but currently give little space to environmental risks; that should change so fiscal risks include climate-related scenarios.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: On targets: the Seventh Carbon Budget set costs for decarbonisation. Do we need similar clear delivery and financing plans for nature?

turns.speaker: Professor Jacobs
turns.text: Yes. A key legal difference matters: the Climate Change Act’s carbon targets are legally binding; Environment Act targets are not—so they lack the same enforcement power.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: How do we handle benefits that fall to a different Department or to households, like retrofit saving health and social costs?

turns.speaker: Jill Rutter
turns.text: This is a cross-government problem. If a policy is a clear prime‑ministerial priority and a Department pushes it, you get progress. Otherwise Departments fear spending for other people’s gains.

chapters.title: Institutional fixes: cross-department units and delivery tools
chapters.takeaway: Better cross-government institutions—joint offices, strategy and delivery units, and ringfenced prevention budgets—would align incentives and improve delivery.

turns.speaker: Professor Jacobs
turns.text: Bring Treasury officials into policy formation. The Office of Climate Change (OCC) in 2007 was an effective cross‑departmental model that built buy-in and innovation.

turns.speaker: Jill Rutter
turns.text: Joint co‑production is missing now. Departments often find Treasury initiatives have overtaken their work because the Budget can fast-track measures.

turns.speaker: Professor Jacobs
turns.text: We used to have Public Service Agreement targets in spending reviews, with named accounting officers and cross-department responsibility. That structure helped hold people accountable.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: Should the Treasury publish environmental impact assessments again like in 2021?

turns.speaker: Jill Rutter
turns.text: Publication matters only if it affects decisions. Ask the Treasury whether those assessments changed outcomes or were just compliance paperwork.

turns.speaker: Chris Hinchliff
turns.text: Is the Treasury’s orthodox economic thinking equipped to handle escalating climate risks that already impose large costs?

turns.speaker: Professor Jacobs
turns.text: If political priority rises, yes. But economists often discount the future; Green Book and value-for-money rules must be used to make adaptation a priority now.

turns.speaker: Jill Rutter
turns.text: We recommend wiring climate resilience into accounting officers’ duties so every Department must test spending for climate risk and future retrofit costs.

turns.speaker: Chris Hinchliff
turns.text: Should the OBR and Bank of England change approach to reflect these risks?

turns.speaker: Professor Jacobs
turns.text: OBR is constrained by fiscal rules and its model; the Bank has an independent role and has done more under some governors than others. Both relationships with government should be reviewed.

turns.speaker: Jill Rutter
turns.text: Don’t overburden the OBR. It’s small and technical; government and national risk bodies should lead horizon-scanning, with the OBR reflecting risks in fiscal analysis.

chapters.title: Practical recommendations and accountability
chapters.takeaway: Fix scoring horizons, create cross‑department strategy and delivery units, set binding targets where possible, ringfence prevention budgets, and make accounting officers responsible for climate resilience.

turns.speaker: John Whitby
turns.text: Does the Treasury have levers to deliver cross-department priorities, or should the centre do more?

turns.speaker: Jill Rutter
turns.text: The centre should. The new Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet (OPMC) could drive priorities and co‑ordinate with the Treasury, rather than expecting Treasury to deliver everything.

turns.speaker: Professor Jacobs
turns.text: Put strategy and delivery functions in OPMC: a strategy unit to develop ideas and a delivery unit to check progress. That combination worked in earlier governments.

turns.speaker: Julia Buckley
turns.text: Does No.10 North help regional alignment for growth and climate policy?

turns.speaker: Professor Jacobs
turns.text: Yes—combined authorities and regional bodies are where land use, emergencies and many resilience issues are handled; No.10 North can co‑ordinate but they must be resourced.

turns.speaker: Julia Buckley
turns.text: How to ensure monitoring feeds back into funding decisions?

turns.speaker: Jill Rutter
turns.text: Use independent bodies like the adaptation sub-committee and regular league tables to pressure Departments; assign political costs for poor preparedness.

turns.speaker: Professor Jacobs
turns.text: Use a dedicated prevention budget—announced in the Budget—to fund resilience. Clarify its criteria and let Parliament and this Committee scrutinise it.

turns.speaker: Jill Rutter
turns.text: An idea: charge Departments an insurance-style risk premium in their budgets that falls if they invest to reduce future risk. That would make contingent liabilities visible.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Final thoughts?

turns.speaker: Jill Rutter
turns.text: The Treasury’s powers matter, but government-wide political leadership, institutional design to join up Departments, and clearer long-term scoring are what will unlock investment.

turns.speaker: Professor Jacobs
turns.text: Recommend: review OBR modelling horizons, reinstate cross‑department targets or binding delivery plans, set clear prevention budgets, and put strategy and delivery functions in OPMC.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you both—this will help shape our recommendations and the next session with Ministers.
